headline: Ryōshi “should” be gyoshi: the ryō comes from confusion with 猟, which means hunting.

sources.quote: The spelling is likely from Middle Chinese compound 漁師 /渔师 (ngjo srij, literally “fishing + master”). Compare modern Mandarin 漁師 /渔师 (yúshī, “fisherman”).

The expected reading would be gyoshi. The kan'yōyomi (irregular but customary reading) ryō for the character 漁 is from confusion with 猟, whose most common on reading is ryō and means hunting, as used in the homophonic term 猟(りょう)師(し) (ryōshi, “hunter”).

headline: Na, “name”, is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *na; compare Okinawan nā.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *na (compare Okinawan 名 (nā)).

meaning: to draw, to depict, to describe
headline: Egaku is 絵 (e, “picture”) plus 書く (kaku, “write”): literally “to write a picture”.

sources.quote: /weɡaku/ > /eɡaku/
Compound of 絵 (e, “picture”) + 書く (kaku, “write”). Literally "to write a picture", ie, "to draw". The kaku changes to gaku as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Hikari is the nominalized stem of the verb 光る (hikaru, “to shine, to glitter, to gleam”).

sources.quote: ⟨pi₁kari⟩ → */pʲikari/ → /ɸikari/ → /hikari/
From Old Japanese.
Nominalization of the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 光(ひか)る (hikaru, “to shine, to glitter, to gleam”).

headline: Wasureru is from Old Japanese 忘る (wasuru), from Proto-Japonic *wasuru.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 忘る (wasuru), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern, from Proto-Japonic *wasuru.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

headline: Jitai is 字 (“character”) plus 体 (“form”).

sources.quote: 字 (“character”) + 体 (“form”)

headline: Shinken originally meant “real sword”, 真劍, before shifting to mean serious.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 真劍 (MC tsyin kjaemH, “real sword”). Compare modern Mandarin 真劍／真剑 (zhēnjiàn).
The original meaning was real sword. Over time, this shifted, and the term is now often used to mean serious.

headline: Wabiru is cognate with 侘びる (wabiru).

sources.quote: Cognate with Japanese 侘びる (wabiru).

headline: Zonjiru shifted from the verb 存ず (zonzu).

sources.quote: Shift from verb 存ず (zonzu).
Natural progression from サ行変格活用 (sa-gyō henkaku katsuyō, “s-irregular conjugation”) verbs ending in -uru to 上一段活用 (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

headline: Juyō is from Middle Chinese 需要 (MC sju 'jiewH).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 需要 (MC sju 'jiewH).

headline: Tatoeba is the irregular -ba conditional of 例える (tatoeru, “to liken one thing to another”), attested by the Kokin Wakashū of about 920 CE.

sources.quote: Analyzable as the irregular -ba conditional conjugation of verb 例える (tatoeru, “to compare something, to liken one thing to another, to make a metaphor about something”).

Historically, the term appears from at least the late Heian period in the Kokin Wakashū dated roughly 920 CE, indicating that the original derivation was as the regular -ba conditional conjugation of Old Japanese-derived verb 例ふ (tatofu), conjugated in the 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern. Through regular historical processes, classical 例ふ (tatofu) evolved into modern 例える (tatoeru).

headline: Tsubasa is possibly a shift from 鳥 (to, “bird”) plus 総 (fusa, “tassel”), though the vowel change is irregular.

sources.quote: /tubasa/ → /t͡subasa/
From Old Japanese.
Possibly a shift from a compound of 鳥(と) (to, “bird”) + 総(ふさ) (fusa, “tassel”), though the vowel change is irregular.

headline: Karera is 彼 (kare) plus 等 (-ra).

sources.quote: 彼(かれ) (kare) + 等(ら) (-ra)

headline: Madoguchi is 窓 (mado, “window”) plus 口 (kuchi, “mouth, opening”), with kuchi voiced to guchi.

sources.quote: 窓(まど) (mado, “window”) + 口(くち) (kuchi, “mouth, opening”).
The kuchi changes to guchi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Kechi is a shift from 怪事 (keji, “unfortunate event”), and in the Edo period meant “a shabby, lowborn individual”.

sources.quote: Shift from 怪事 (keji, “unfortunate event”). Used in the Edo period to mean "a shabby, lowborn individual" before taking on the current sense.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 尋ぬ (tazunu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

meaning: to freeze, to be frozen over, to congeal
headline: Kōru is from Old Japanese 凍る (koporu), likely cognate with words for hard and stiff such as 凝る (koru, “to stiffen”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 凍る (koporu).

Likely cognate with other terms beginning with ko- and related to senses of hard, stiff, such as 凝(こ)る (koru, “to stiffen”), 凍(こ)ゆ (koyu, “to freeze, to become frozen”, classical) → modern 凍(こご)える (kogoeru), 強(こわ)い (kowai, “hard, tough, stiff”).

headline: Riku, “land”, is from Middle Chinese 陸, first attested as a standalone noun in the mid-1400s.

sources.quote: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 陸 (MC ljuwk). First attested in Japanese as a standalone noun in a text from the mid-1400s.

headline: Kyōkasho is shortened from 教科用図書 (kyōka-yō tosho).

sources.quote: Shortened from 教科用(きょうかよう)図書(としょ) (kyōka-yō tosho).

sources.quote: Most likely of onomatopoeic origin; compare すきすき (sukisuki, “refreshingly”) and すきっと (sukitto, “refreshingly”).

headline: Kasai is from Middle Chinese 火災, and went from kwasai to kasai.

sources.quote: /kwasai/ → /kasai/
From Middle Chinese compound 火災 (xwa^X tsoj). Compare modern Mandarin reading huǒzāi.

headline: Akari originally meant natural light; the lamp sense was expressed with 灯火 (tomoshibi, literally “set alight + fire”).

sources.quote: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 明(あ)かる (akaru, “to become bright”).

This term originally referred to natural light, while the sense of lamp or lighting was expressed using the term 灯火 (tomoshibi, literally “set alight + fire”). The term akari gained its modern lighting sense during the late Edo period, and has now largely displaced tomoshibi for this sense.

headline: Naisen is 内 (nai, “internal”) plus 線 (sen, “line”).

sources.quote: 内(ない) (nai, “internal”) + 線(せん) (sen, “line”)

Related to Baekje ホカ (*poka, “outside”), compare Korean 밖 (bak, “outside”).
